content:
We have discussed the issue of USB-C cables many times: they may look identical on the outside, but their actual performance can vary dramatically.

Google solved this problem in Chrome OS years ago, and we recommended at the time that Apple follow suit. Apple has still not done so, but there is now a free Mac app called WhatCable that can turn your Mac into a hardware cable tester...

Today, almost every electronic device we buy comes with a USB-C cable, which makes it easy to accumulate a whole drawer of cables at home without knowing which one to use when. Each cable has different limits in the following areas:

  • Data transfer speed
  • Video bandwidth
  • Power delivery capability

Cable performance can vary hugely: the best support 40Gb/s data transfer, 8K 60Hz video output, and 240W power delivery; the worst are charge-only cables, as well as slow cables with data transfer speeds of only 480Mbps.

Hardware cable testers are available for purchase that can report the capabilities of connected cables, but there is now a free Mac app that does the same thing. WhatCable works by measuring the actual performance of a cable in use, or — as the joke about "a Mac charging itself" goes — connecting a cable from one USB-C port on the Mac to another.

It can also read identification data from chips embedded in the cable to determine the manufacturer and whether the cable is USB-IF certified. Note that lack of certification does not necessarily mean a cable is counterfeit — the manufacturer may simply have chosen not to pay the certification fee.

This app works because Macs already read these capability details from embedded chips. WhatCable makes accessing this information easy and translates everything into plain, understandable language.

See whether your current charging speed is being limited by the cable, the charger, or the Mac itself, and understand the negotiated power delivery specifications. In plain language, determine whether the Mac port, cable, or device is the bottleneck, so you know whether switching to a faster cable will actually help. When connecting a display, see whether you are getting the full resolution and refresh rate, or whether these are being reduced, and whether the limitation comes from the adapter, cable, or the mode you have selected. Decode cable speed, current rating, manufacturer identity, and USB PD capability markers from marked USB-C cables

The free version includes all of the above features, while the Pro version offers more detailed information, such as real-time negotiation details for each connection, showing how and why two devices end up operating at a particular charging or transfer speed. The Pro version is a one-time purchase priced at £9.99 (approximately US$13.40).

The Verge's Sean Hollister tried it out and thought it worked well, although not perfectly, because some cables misrepresent their capabilities.
